Xi Song is Professor of Sociology at Columbia University. Her research focuses on social mobility, occupations and work, Asian Americans, population, and computational methods. She earned a BA in Sociology from Renmin University of China in 2008 and an MPhil from The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology in 2010. She then received both an MS in Statistics and a Ph.D. in Sociology from the University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA) in 2015. She is a member of the Sociological Research Association and received the William Julius Wilson Early Career Award from the American Sociological Association (ASA) in 2021.

Youngjoo Cha is Professor of Sociology at Indiana University-Bloomington. Her current research investigates how the trend toward long work hours and the normative forces behind it reinforce gender inequality and what organizational practices and conditions that can mitigate these impacts. Her work also explores the relationship between parenthood and the gender wage gap, how cultural norms surrounding ideal workers and ideal parents shape the consequences of using flexible work practices, and the role of stereotypes for the labor market outcomes for individuals of Asian origin in the U.S.

Ohjae Gowen is an Assistant Professor of Sociology (ABD) at Singapore Management University. His research focuses on work-family dynamics and their implications for gender inequality and demographic behavior. He received his Ph.D. in Sociology from Harvard University in 2024.


Ryota Mugiyama is an Associate Professor in the Department of Political Studies at Gakushuin University. His research focuses on labor market inequality, intergenerational mobility, and family formation. He received his Doctorate in Sociology from the University of Tokyo in 2019.

Leafia Ye is an Assistant Professor of Sociology at the University of Toronto. She received her Ph.D. in Sociology from the University of Wisconsin-Madison, and a Bachelor’s degree in Sociology and German from the University of Hong Kong. She is broadly interested in inequalities by immigration status and in the aging process. She’s currently the Principal Investigator of the project “immigrant integration and later-life health,” which is funded by the U.S. National Institutes of Health.


Tate Kihara is an Assistant Professor in the Graduate School of Media and Governance at Keio University. His research examines international migration to and from Japan in both historical and contemporary contexts, with a particular focus on its relationship to social inequality. He earned his Ph.D. in Sociology from Brown University in 2023.

title: SSM2025 Research
text:
Research outputs of the 2025 Social Stratification and Social Mobility Survey (SSM2025) research group, based at the Institute of Social Science, The University of Tokyo.
The SSM survey is Japan’s longest-running nationally representative survey of social stratification and mobility. It has been carried out every ten years since 1955, and the 2025 survey is the eighth wave. The series makes it possible to trace how class structure, educational attainment, occupational careers, and intergenerational mobility in Japan have changed over seventy years.

title: About the Survey
text: The Social Stratification and Social Mobility (SSM) survey has been conducted every ten years since 1955 by research groups of Japanese sociologists. Its core questions—respondents’ occupational histories, educational attainment, and parents’ occupations and education—have been asked in a comparable form across waves, which makes the series a central resource for the study of inequality and mobility in Japan. SSM2025 is the eighth wave.

title: About the Survey
text: The Social Stratification and Social Mobility (SSM) survey has been conducted every ten years since 1955 by research groups of Japanese sociologists. Its core questions—respondents’ occupational histories, educational attainment, and parents’ occupations and education—have been asked in a comparable form across waves, which makes the series a central resource for the study of inequality and mobility in Japan. SSM2025 is the eighth wave.

title: About the Survey
text:
SSM2025 design

Population: residents of Japan aged 20–79
Sampling: stratified two-stage random sampling (650 sampling points) from the Basic Resident Registers
Modes: face-to-face interviews combined with a self-administered (drop-off) questionnaire, with a self-administered mail follow-up
Main content: current and first occupation, full occupational history, education, parents’ and spouse’s occupations and education, family formation, income, and social attitudes

The SSM2025 project also includes a survey of young adults, a regional survey, a survey of foreign residents, and a follow-up survey of respondents (autumn 2026).

title: About the Survey
text:
Research organization

Survey design: The 2025 SSM Survey Research Group
Principal investigators: Sho Fujihara and Kikuko Nagayoshi (Institute of Social Science, The University of Tokyo)
Funding: JSPS Grant-in-Aid for Specially Promoted Research (JP23H05402)

title: About the Survey
text:
Data access
The SSM2025 data are currently being cleaned and coded, and are available only to members of the research group. Plans for public release will be announced on this site.

title: About the Survey
text:
Acknowledging the data
Publications using SSM2025 data should state that the data come from the 2025 Social Stratification and Social Mobility Survey and that the survey was supported by JSPS KAKENHI Grant Number JP23H05402.

Emma Zang is an Assistant Professor of Sociology at Yale University, with secondary appointments in Biostatistics and Global Affairs. Her research focuses on family demography, aging, health disparities, and social policy, using advanced quantitative and computational methods. She leads several interdisciplinary projects funded by NIH and other agencies, and her work has been featured in leading academic journals and major media outlets. She received her Ph.D. in Public Policy from Duke University.


Takuma Kamada is an Associate Professor at the University of Osaka, Osaka School of International Public Policy (OSIPP) in Japan. His research seeks to understand the causes and consequences of crime and its enforcement. In particular, he studies (i) how both criminal and non-criminal justice policies affect crime and (ii) how drug epidemics shape cities and neighborhoods, with a particular emphasis on illegal markets in different ethno-racial contexts.

Ian Lundberg is an Assistant Professor in the Department of Sociology at UCLA, where he co-directs the Inequality Data Science Lab and is an affiliate of the California Center for Population Research and the Center for Social Statistics. He received a PhD in sociology and social policy at Princeton University in 2021. Ian’s research develops statistical methods to answer new questions about inequality and social stratification, often focusing on causal inference.


Shoki Okubo is an Assistant Professor of Sociology at Toyo University in Japan. His research focuses on three main areas: (1) improving the internal and external validity of survey statistics and methodology; (2) advancing the theory and application of causal inference; and (3) examining how long-term care and health insurance systems in Japan influence both the providers and recipients of care and medical services.
